forms.detail: EUDA drug profile: synthetic cannabinoids appeared in herbal smoking mixtures in late 2008, sold in metal-foil sachets of 3 g of dried vegetable matter, and also as incense or room odorisers. Product names it lists: Spice Gold, Spice Silver, Spice Diamond, Yucatan Fire, Sence, Chill X, Smoke, Genie, Algerian Blend.

DEA fact sheet: often sold as 'herbal incense' or 'potpourri'; synthetic cannabinoids sprayed or mixed onto plant material, and liquids made to be vaporized in electronic cigarettes. Federal Register (2011): marketed as herbal incense or plant food (one named 'Bonsai-18'), in small pouches or packets labelled 'Not For Human Consumption'.

EMCDDA risk assessment (November 2017): most often herbal or plant material, including branded 'legal high' products, then powder, and to a lesser extent liquids (including e-liquids) and blotters; a white solid when pure. About 100 kg of herbal material (74 kg in Turkey) and about 13 kg of powder were seized; the largest single seizure was about 2.3 kg of powder (French customs, 2017); the United Kingdom reported 129 seizures (about 3 kg) in prisons. DEA Diversion Control Division (May 2019): marketed under the guise of herbal incense products and laced on plant material.

EMCDDA risk assessment (December 2020): powders, smoking mixtures (herbal material or tobacco), impregnated paper (blotters and cards) and liquids or e-liquids; 770 seizures by November 2020, including about 47 kg of powder and 4.7 kg of smoking mixtures. WHO ECDD (October 2020): described as a white, yellow/brown or tan powder; found in herbal material, in paper infused with it that was mailed into Scottish prisons, in e-liquids and blotters, and in products sold as heroin or as cannabis/THC.

WHO ECDD (October 2022): the pure substance is typically a beige or yellowish powder; it has been found on plant material or blotting paper sprayed with solutions of it, in adulterated cannabis or hemp plant material, in paper infused with it and in powders.
